cards.explanation: The answer is mouth, friends. David says, "I will watch my ways so that I will not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle…" (Psalm 39:1). He says the guarding is so he will not sin with his tongue. Honestly, we've all had a moment where a muzzle would've saved us a whole conversation.

The answer is False, friends. The text says David "…remained silent, even from speaking good…" (Psalm 39:2). The muzzle didn't sort his words into good and bad. It just shut the whole shop. And the verse adds that his sorrow was stirred.

The answer is that his heart grows hot within him, friends. David says, "My heart grew hot within me; as I mused, the fire burned." (Psalm 39:3). He kept it all in, and the inside didn't stay quiet. I think anybody who's ever held in a big feeling knows that heat. Then he finally speaks.

The first thing David asks the LORD to show him is his end and the measure of his days, friends. He prays, "Show me, O LORD, my end and the measure of my days. Let me know how fleeting my life is." (Psalm 39:4). After all that silence, you might expect a complaint about the wicked. Instead he asks about how short life is. That's a surprise, and I like it.

The answer is short, friends. David says, "You, indeed, have made my days as handbreadths…" (Psalm 39:5). A handbreadth is about the width of your hand, and that's a tiny measure for a whole life. He even asked to know "…how fleeting my life is." (Psalm 39:4). Hold up your hand and look at it for a second.

David is saying it all comes to nothing, friends. He says every man "…bustles in vain…" and "…heaps up riches not knowing who will haul them away." (Psalm 39:6). All that rushing around, and he doesn't even know who ends up with the pile. It's like a man who packs a cookie box for months and has no idea whose table it lands on.

The answer is True, friends! David asks, "And now, O Lord, for what do I wait?" and then answers himself right away: "My hope is in You." (Psalm 39:7). After talking about breath and phantoms, he lands on the one place he puts his hope. I think that's the turn of the whole psalm.

The answer is the Lord, friends. David says, "I have become mute; I do not open my mouth because of what You have done." (Psalm 39:9). He's speaking to the Lord, and he points to what the Lord has done. The fools and the friends aren't the reason here.

The answer is False, friends. The verse says the Lord is "…consuming like a moth what he holds dear; surely each man is but a vapor." (Psalm 39:11). A moth doesn't ask permission, it just eats the sweater. So what a man holds dear isn't safe.

The answer is all his fathers, friends. David says, "For I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers." (Psalm 39:12). He puts himself in the same line as his fathers. He calls them strangers, just like him.

David asks the LORD to turn His gaze away from him, friends. He prays, "Turn Your gaze away from me, that I may again be cheered before I depart and am no more." (Psalm 39:13). It's a heavy way to end a psalm, and I think this one hurts. He asks to be cheered again before his days are done.
